METHODS & LIMITATIONS

From hydraulic response to a leak signal.

This prototype extends Mansi Aher’s original two-zone EPANET network into an interactive experiment. Its newly trained detector and evaluation are separate from the thesis results.

1. Simulate the network

The original network contains a reservoir, an outlet tank, two fixture zones, six sensor locations, and parallel pressure-reducing valves. Pipe lengths, diameters, elevations, roughness, demands, and valve settings are retained. The interface is a simplified schematic; it does not draw the parallel valves.

WNTR invokes EPANET 2.2 to solve each steady-state hydraulic condition. Leaks are junction emitters: Q = C × √P. The three openings use coefficients 0.0001, 0.0003, and 0.001 m³/s/√m. These are emitter coefficients, not hole diameters. All displayed pressures use metres of water head.

The browser selects from 57 precomputed hydraulic states: three demand levels, each with one baseline and eighteen leak scenarios. Changing the controls selects exact simulations; it does not interpolate or solve hydraulics in the browser.

2. Build an observation sequence

Each experiment contains 30 observation steps. For leak experiments, steps 0–9 use the no-leak state and steps 10–29 use the leak state. Independent, zero-mean Gaussian sensor noise is added with the selected standard deviation. A saved seed reproduces the sequence.

This abrupt switch between steady states is not a hydraulic transient simulation. Steps do not represent seconds or minutes, and detection delay is reported only in observation steps.

3. Detect a pressure change

The six model inputs are baseline pressure minus observed pressure at each sensor. The Random Forest contains 48 trees with maximum depth 7 and at least 5 training samples per leaf. It does not receive leak location, emitter coefficient, or the true label. A score of 0.5 or above is a positive observation. Detection delay requires three consecutive positive observations after onset. False alarms count individual positive observations during no-leak steps, rather than sustained alert events.

The baseline uses the same demand as the experiment. This assumes demand is known and a matched healthy baseline is available. Unknown demand changes, drifting sensors, and network topology changes are not tested. The displayed model score is the mean tree probability, not calibrated confidence.

4. Evaluate on separate operating conditions

Training uses demand multipliers 0.6, 0.85, 1.15, and 1.4 and five emitter coefficients. Evaluation uses 0.7, 1.0, and 1.3 and three different coefficients. Noisy copies of one hydraulic condition do not cross the split. Both sets use the same network and sensor locations; this is not validation on unseen networks or physical hardware.

Loading evaluation…

The evaluation set is balanced between leak and no-leak observations, with noise sampled from 0 to 0.5 m. Its precision will not necessarily hold when leaks are rare. These metrics evaluate single observations; the three-observation alert rule is demonstrated separately in each replay.

Download the full evaluation record

What remains to establish

  • Performance with unknown demand, sensor bias, dropout, and time-correlated noise.
  • Evaluation on an independently held-out network and physical sensor data.
  • Extended-period hydraulics, rather than replaying steady states.
  • A deployed simulation service for arbitrary operating conditions.

Current saved experiments stay in this browser on this device. There is no account, cloud notebook, or live physical network connection.
